justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'd assume was a recent price level around 304–305, based on typical mean-reversion and drift dynamics for a financial asset trading in this range. For the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the last observed price with only a small positive drift, reflecting the general tendency for short-term prices to stay near their recent level while acknowledging slight bullish momentum. For the one-week estimate, I nudged the forecast slightly higher to around 307, incorporating a small expected drift while keeping the estimate conservative. For the one-month horizon, I projected a further modest increase to 310, reflecting longer-term drift assumptions and the general tendency of risk assets to trend slightly upward over time when no strong bearish signals are present.

The confidence interval widths were driven primarily by the time horizon itself, following the square-root-of-time scaling that characterizes random walk uncertainty. At one day, the interval is relatively tight at roughly plus or minus 10 points, reflecting limited time for new information to accumulate. By one week, the interval widens to about plus or minus 20 points, and by one month it expands to plus or minus 40 points, capturing the compounding uncertainty over a longer period. I also factored in typical volatility levels for an asset in this price range, which suggested moderate but not extreme daily fluctuations.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include sudden macroeconomic announcements such as unexpected inflation prints, central bank policy shifts, or geopolitical shocks, any of which could generate moves well beyond a single standard deviation in a short period. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst like strong earnings, a policy pivot, or a major liquidity injection could push the one-month outcome above 350. On the downside, a risk-off event, credit stress, or broader market selloff could easily breach the lower bound of 270.

It is worth noting that my intervals, while covering 90% of the probability mass under my model assumptions, are still model-dependent. Real-world distributions of financial returns tend to have fat tails, meaning extreme events occur more frequently than a normal distribution would predict. This means the true probability of outcomes outside my stated ranges is likely somewhat higher than the nominal 10% implied by a 90% confidence interval.
